hardware_summary: Frame 7-class gas turbines directly shaft-drive the propane and mixed-refrigerant (MR) compression trains on operating Trains 1-3; no electricity is generated by these units. The proposed Train 4 expansion replaces this with 3x electric (E-Drive) motors, up to 75 MW each.
fuel_basis: Boil-off/flash gas from the LNG process fuels the 'propane and MR gas turbine driven compression cycles' per Cameron LNG's own technical page; Gas Compression Magazine confirms these are 'Frame 7 gas turbine drives' on the existing trains.
captive_summary: Cameron LNG's operating Trains 1-3 use on-site gas turbine mechanical drive (Frame 7-class) to directly shaft-drive the propane and mixed-refrigerant refrigeration compressors. This is captive gas power under the mechanical-drive test even though no electricity is generated. The proposed Train 4 unit is a different case: its FERC-amended design replaces the gas turbines with three electric motors (up to 75 MW each) specifically to cut emissions, so Train 4 itself is NOT captive gas power.
mechanical_drive_note: Frame 7-class gas turbines (typical installed shaft power ~190 MW per train per trade literature) driving propane and MR compressor strings on Trains 1-3; Train 4 (proposed) instead uses 3x E-Drive electric motors capped at 75 MW each.
confirmed_how: Cameron LNG's own site (cameronlng.com/lng-facility/lng-and-liquefaction/) states flash/boil-off gas fuels 'the propane and MR gas turbine driven compression cycles.' Gas Compression Magazine (2022-03-21), reporting on the FERC-filed Train 4 design amendment, states the existing design uses 'Frame 7 gas turbine drives' for the refrigerant compressors, and that Train 4 replaces them with 'three E-Drive motors...limited to 75 MW for the project to remain within a proven size range.'

Woodside Louisiana LNG Terminal power station (6.26 km, construction, GOGPT-captive) is the captive plant for the separate, adjacent Woodside Louisiana LNG project, not Cameron LNG. Calcasieu power station (13.96 km, operating, GOGPT non-captive) is an unrelated merchant plant. Neither belongs to Cameron LNG. (info: https://lngprime.com/americas/cameron-lng-entergy-advance-renewable-power-deal/68301/ confirms Cameron LNG itself is on an Entergy grid-power arrangement for its non-mechanical-drive electric loads, consistent with the two GOGPT neighbors being unrelated third-party plants.)
gogpt_candidate_basis: Cameron LNG's captive gas turbines are mechanical-drive only (shaft power, zero MWe) — this is not an electricity-generating station GOGPT would track under its own name. GOGPT already separately tracks the neighboring, unrelated Woodside Louisiana LNG Terminal power station for that different project.
status_or_other_findings: Train 4 (currently `proposed` in GEM) uses electric drive motors rather than gas turbines, per the FERC-amended design covered by Gas Compression Magazine (2022) and ESG Review's coverage of the same filing — a design detail relevant if/when Train 4 is later built, but not itself a captive-power finding.

captive_summary: Cook Inlet LNG (a Gardes Holdings unit) is an early-stage FSRU import project proposed to moor alongside the existing offshore Osprey platform in Alaska's Cook Inlet, with FERC pre-filing only just initiated (first gas targeted mid-2029). No FSRU vessel has been named or selected in any public source found, and no source describes onboard power generation, dual-fuel engines, or grid connection. This is genuinely undisclosed, not a documented negative.
confirmed_how: LNG Prime, GIIGNL news, Gas Processing & LNG, Petroleum News, and Offshore Energy all describe only the regasification throughput (up to 300 MMscf/day design capacity, ~22 Bcf/yr initial phase) and the mooring plan alongside the existing Osprey platform; none names a selected FSRU vessel or its power equipment. Cook Inlet LNG's own site (cookinletlng.com) gives only capacity/process-flow description, no power-generation detail.
gogpt_prior_assessment: Nikiski cogeneration power station (16.24 km, GOGPT non-captive, operating) is an existing Alaska Railbelt utility cogeneration plant unrelated to the proposed Cook Inlet FSRU, which would in any case be moored offshore at the existing Osprey platform, not co-located with Nikiski. Info: https://www.offshore-energy.biz/cook-inlet-lng-puts-new-fsru-based-lifeline-on-alaskas-energy-horizon/ (confirms the Osprey-platform mooring location, distinct from Nikiski).
gogpt_candidate_basis: No power generation of any kind is documented for this project yet; nothing to add at this stage.
status_or_other_findings: Project is in the earliest stage of FERC pre-filing as of the underlying reporting; first gas targeted mid-2029. Design throughput up to 300 MMscf/day (approx. 110 bcf/yr full design capacity), with an initial phase around 22 Bcf/yr.
notes: FSRU-onboard convention would apply once a specific vessel is named — re-check in a future batch once FERC pre-filing documents or a vessel selection are published.

captive_summary: Creole Trail LNG Terminal was a mid-2000s Cheniere-era LNG receiving/import terminal proposal in the Cameron Parish, Louisiana corridor that received early FERC review but was never built. GEM's own record shows the unit `cancelled`/`inferred 4 y` — consistent with a long-dormant proposal. No engineering-level (FEED/EPC) design describing power generation, vaporization equipment, or any turbine/generator hardware could be found in any accessible public source; the project never advanced past an early-2000s regulatory filing.
confirmed_how: Available secondary coverage (SEC filings, FERC-era reporting) describes only that a receiving terminal in the Creole Trail/Cameron Parish corridor was approved alongside the separate (and actually-built) Creole Trail Pipeline; no subsequent EPC contractor release, equipment-vendor press release, or technical filing describing power/vaporization equipment was found for the terminal itself.
gogpt_prior_assessment: Both neighboring GOGPT plants — Calcasieu Pass 2 power plant (14.6 km, GOGPT-captive, construction/pre-construction) and Calcasieu Pass LNG Terminal power station (15.5 km, GOGPT-captive, operating) — are the captive power stations of the separate, unrelated, and actually-built Calcasieu Pass / Calcasieu Pass 2 LNG projects, not of this long-dormant, never-built Creole Trail proposal.
gogpt_candidate_basis: No design or hardware for this terminal was ever published; nothing to add. The neighboring GOGPT records already correctly belong to different, built projects.
status_or_other_findings: GEM shows this unit `cancelled` with substatus `inferred 4 y`, consistent with a dormant, never-progressed proposal; no revival activity found.
notes: Not to be confused with the built and operating Creole Trail Pipeline (a 94-mile pipeline linking Sabine Pass LNG to interstate pipelines) — that is separate pipeline infrastructure, not this terminal record.

captive_summary: Crown Landing was a well-advanced (BP-sponsored, FERC-approved 2006, FEIS completed) LNG import/regasification terminal proposal in Gloucester County, NJ (pier partly in New Castle County, DE), with a real published design — 450,000 m3 of LNG storage and 1.2 Bcf/d baseload send-out via the new 11-mile Logan Lateral pipeline — but Hess (BP's successor) surrendered the FERC authorization in January 2012 citing reduced import need from US shale gas growth, and the project was never built. No source found describes on-site power generation, vaporization method (SCV/ORV/seawater), or any turbine/generator equipment for the facility.
confirmed_how: Wikipedia (citing Hess Corp/FERC record) and NaturalGasIntel's original coverage describe capacity, storage, and pipeline details but neither mentions power generation equipment. FERC's own EIS page for the project could not be accessed (403) in this research pass.
gogpt_prior_assessment: Neither neighboring GOGPT plant is related. Camden Plant Holdings power station (2.9 km, GOGPT non-captive, operating) and Eagle Point power generation (4.1 km, GOGPT non-captive, operating) are existing merchant power stations in the Delaware River industrial corridor, unconnected to the cancelled, never-built Crown Landing terminal.
gogpt_candidate_basis: No power generation is documented for the project at all; nothing to add.
status_or_other_findings: Terminal authorization surrendered/withdrawn by Hess in January 2012, citing reduced import need from the shale gas boom; GEM's `cancelled`/`inferred 4y` status is consistent with this.

hardware_summary: A dedicated on-site 'gas-powered power plant' was a named, distinct component of the published project design (alongside 12 planned liquefaction units and a marine loading berth); no turbine model, unit count, or MW rating was found in any accessible source.
fuel_basis: Described as 'gas-powered' in trade press covering the project's design and June 2025 FERC withdrawal; consistent with Venture Global's design pattern at its sibling Plaquemines and Calcasieu Pass terminals, both of which have GOGPT-tracked, GOGPT-confirmed-captive on-site gas power stations (up to 2,860 MW and 720 MW respectively).
captive_summary: Delta LNG (Venture Global, Plaquemines Parish, LA) was withdrawn from FERC pre-filing in June 2025 in favor of expanding the adjacent Plaquemines LNG terminal, but its published project design explicitly included 'a gas-powered power plant' as a named, distinct component alongside 12 liquefaction units and a loading berth. As-designed captive power on a cancelled/unbuilt project still counts as a YES; no MW figure or equipment detail was found in any source I could verify, so `electric_mw` is left blank rather than assumed.
confirmed_how: Offshore Technology (reporting Venture Global's June 2025 FERC withdrawal) states the project 'entails constructing 12 liquefaction units, a loading berth and a gas-powered power plant,' describing the filed project's components.

gogpt_prior_assessment: Plaquemines LNG Terminal power station (1.39 km, GOGPT-captive, ~2,860 MW aggregate) is the confirmed captive plant for the adjacent, separate, already-operating Plaquemines LNG terminal (also Venture Global) — a different GEM terminal record, not Delta LNG's own (cancelled, never-built) design. gogpt_candidate_basis: A cogeneration/on-site power plant is confirmed by the design description, but MW rating and unit count are undisclosed and the project was formally withdrawn before final engineering — unclear whether GOGPT would create a record for a project the sponsor has withdrawn from FERC review.
status_or_other_findings: Venture Global formally withdrew Delta LNG's FERC pre-filing application on 2025-06-10, redirecting investment to the Plaquemines LNG expansion instead; GEM's `cancelled` status is consistent and well-documented.

captive_summary: Downeast LNG was originally filed with FERC in 2006 as a standard LNG import/regasification terminal in Washington County, Maine, then in 2014 the sponsor sought to convert it to a bidirectional import/export facility. The conversion never advanced past pre-filing, and FERC dismissed/terminated all dockets in August 2016 citing 'no significant recent progress' after the project was listed for sale. No engineering-level design for on-site power generation (which would only be relevant to the never-developed export/liquefaction conversion) was ever published.
confirmed_how: LNG Industry and Offshore Energy (2016) report FERC's dismissal of the dockets for lack of recent progress; DOE's EIS-0508 project page and CBC News confirm the original scope (up to 3 mtpa export / 100 mmcf/d regas capacity) without describing power-generation equipment.
gogpt_prior_assessment: No GOGPT neighbor was found for this terminal_id within 30 km in the neighbors file (sparsely populated Washington County, Maine coast).
gogpt_candidate_basis: No power generation of any kind is documented; nothing to add.
status_or_other_findings: FERC formally dismissed/terminated the dockets in August 2016; DOE separately withdrew its own pending application in April 2017.

captive_summary: Eos FLNG (Eos LNG, founded by Andrew Kunian) was a proposed floating LNG export facility off Brownsville, Texas. DOE granted FTA export authorization in December 2013, and in a September 2014 interview the founder said FERC filings were planned for 2015 — but no FERC filing, FEED study, or further company activity has been found since 2014; the project is presumed abandoned. It is a distinct entity from the nearby, still-active 'Texas LNG' project (Texas LNG Brownsville LLC, FEED by Samsung Engineering 2016) and should not be conflated with it. No engineering-level design was ever published for Eos FLNG, so no captive-power finding is possible.
confirmed_how: EcoWatch's coverage and the absence of any FERC docket, technical filing, or vendor release for 'Eos LNG'/'Eos FLNG' since 2014 (checked against Wikipedia's separate, detailed 'Texas LNG project' article, which confirms Texas LNG is a distinct, still-active project at the same port).
gogpt_prior_assessment: Port Of Brownsville Energy Complex (5.35 km, GOGPT non-captive, pre-construction) and Silas Ray power station (11.8 km, GOGPT non-captive, operating) are unrelated merchant/industrial power projects in the Port of Brownsville area, not tied to the long-abandoned Eos FLNG proposal.
gogpt_candidate_basis: No design of any kind was ever published for this cancelled, never-filed proposal.
status_or_other_findings: Presumed abandoned since 2014; no FERC docket was ever opened despite the December 2013 DOE FTA export authorization.
notes: Do not confuse with 'Texas LNG' / 'Texas LNG Brownsville LLC,' a separate, still-active FERC-authorized project at a different Port of Brownsville site.

captive_summary: Fourchon LNG (the original Energy World-era Port Fourchon proposal) was removed from FERC's pre-filing process in December 2023 for inactivity. The project never advanced past pre-filing to a detailed engineering/FEED design, and no equipment-level source (turbine, generator, or compressor specification) was ever published for it. The site's lease has since passed to a different developer's Argent LNG Terminal project (a separate GEM record), which should not be conflated with this cancelled Fourchon LNG record.
confirmed_how: LNG Prime and Argent LNG's own site describe Argent LNG's June 2024 lease of the Port Fourchon site previously held for the (since-removed) Fourchon LNG proposal; no FEED-level source for the original Fourchon LNG project itself was found in this research pass.
gogpt_prior_assessment: Argent LNG Terminal power station (2.19 km, GOGPT-captive, pre-construction, ~675 MW/5 units) is the power station GOGPT tracks for the successor Argent LNG project at the same Port Fourchon site — it is not this (cancelled, superseded) Fourchon LNG record's own captive power. Bayou power station (12.1 km, GOGPT non-captive, cancelled) is a separate, independently-cancelled merchant project also unrelated to this terminal.
gogpt_candidate_basis: No design was ever published for this specific (now-superseded) project; the site's own power station is already tracked under the successor Argent LNG Terminal record.
status_or_other_findings: FERC removed the project from active pre-filing in December 2023 for inactivity; the site lease was subsequently taken over by Argent LNG (June 2024).
notes: GEM carries this as a separate terminal record from Argent LNG Terminal, which occupies the same physical site under a new developer — worth confirming in a future batch whether these records should be cross-referenced.
